# Concept list
Each concept: its name, a short description, and the lesson that defines it.

- **summation notation** (summation) (Defined in prerequisite)
- **logarithm** (logarithm) (Defined in prerequisite)
- **geometric series** (geometric-series) (Defined in prerequisite)
- **derivative** (derivative) (Defined in prerequisite)
- **time value of money** (time-value-of-money): The same amount of money is worth more the earlier you receive it, so amounts at different times must be moved to the same date before they are compared or added. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **compound interest** (compound-interest): Interest that is added to the principal and earns interest itself. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **future value** (future-value): The amount that a sum today grows to at a future date with compound interest. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **present value** (present-value): The value today of an amount received in the future. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **discount factor** (discount-factor): The number that a future amount is multiplied by to get its present value: 1/(1+r)ⁿ. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **annual percentage rate** (apr): The quoted yearly rate (APR), equal to the rate per period times the number of periods in a year, without compounding within the year. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **effective annual rate** (ear): The yearly rate actually earned once compounding within the year is taken into account (EAR). (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **continuous compounding** (continuous-compounding): The limit when compounding becomes infinitely frequent. Then FV = PV·e^(rT). (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **annuity** (annuity): A finite series of equal payments at equal intervals. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **perpetuity** (perpetuity): Equal payments at equal intervals that continue forever. Its present value is C/r. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **annuity due** (annuity-due): An annuity whose payments are made at the start of each period. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **growing perpetuity** (growing-perpetuity): Payments that grow at a constant rate each period and continue forever. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **simple return** (simple-return): The proportional price change P₁/P₀ − 1. Over several periods, simple returns compound by multiplication. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **log return** (log-return): The natural logarithm of the price ratio, ln(P₁/P₀). Over several periods, log returns add. (Defined in 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money)
- **objective function** (objective-function): The quantity that an optimization problem maximizes or minimizes. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **first-order condition** (first-order-condition): At an interior optimum, the derivative (or every partial derivative) is 0. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **second-order condition** (second-order-condition): The sign of the second derivative tells a maximum from a minimum. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **fixed cost** (fixed-cost): The part of total cost that does not change with output. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **variable cost** (variable-cost): The part of total cost that changes with output. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **marginal revenue** (marginal-revenue): The extra revenue from selling one more unit, that is, the derivative of revenue with respect to output. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **marginal cost** (marginal-cost): The extra cost of producing one more unit, that is, the derivative of cost with respect to output. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **profit maximization** (profit-maximization): Choosing output to make profit as large as possible. At an interior optimum, marginal revenue equals marginal cost. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **sunk cost** (sunk-cost): A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered whatever you decide next. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **partial derivative** (partial-derivative): The rate of change of a function when one variable changes and the others stay fixed. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **budget constraint** (budget-constraint): Total spending cannot exceed the money available, for example px·x + py·y = M with two goods. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **Lagrange multiplier** (lagrange-multiplier): The variable λ introduced to solve an optimization problem with an equality constraint. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **shadow price** (shadow-price): The approximate increase in the optimal value of the objective when the constraint is relaxed by one unit. (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **corner solution** (corner-solution): An optimum at which a choice variable is at its boundary (for example, 0). (Defined in 0.2 Optimization)
- **random variable** (random-variable): A quantity whose value is uncertain but whose possible values and their probabilities are known. (Defined in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance)
- **expected value** (expected-value): The probability-weighted average outcome, that is, the average over many repetitions of the same situation. (Defined in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance)
- **variance** (variance): The probability-weighted average of squared deviations from the expected value. Its unit is the square of the original unit (for example, %²). (Defined in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance)
- **standard deviation** (standard-deviation): The square root of the variance, in the same unit as the variable. In finance it is also called volatility. (Defined in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance)
- **covariance** (covariance): The probability-weighted average of the product of two variables' deviations from their expected values. It is positive when they move in the same direction and negative when they move in opposite directions. (Defined in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance)
- **correlation coefficient** (correlation): The covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations. It has no unit and lies between −1 and 1. (Defined in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance)
- **portfolio variance** (portfolio-variance): The variance of a two-asset portfolio is the sum of each variance times its squared weight, plus a covariance term. (Defined in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance)
- **diversification** (diversification): The benefit a portfolio gets when its standard deviation is lower than the weighted average of the assets' standard deviations. (Defined in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance)
- **probability density** (probability-density): A curve for a continuous random variable; the area under the curve over an interval is the probability of a value in that interval. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **normal distribution** (normal-distribution): A bell-shaped, symmetric distribution that is fully determined by its mean μ and standard deviation σ, written N(μ, σ²). (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **z-score** (z-score): How many standard deviations a value is from the mean: z = (x − μ)/σ. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **fat tails** (fat-tails): Extreme values occur more often than in a normal distribution with the same standard deviation. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **median** (median): The middle value when all outcomes are sorted; half of the outcomes are below it and half above. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **right skew** (right-skew): A distribution with a long tail on the right, so the mean is above the median. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **lognormal distribution** (lognormal-distribution): A distribution whose logarithm is normal; wealth that compounds over many periods is approximately lognormal. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **parameter estimation** (parameter-estimation): Using sample data to infer population parameters, such as the true mean and standard deviation. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **sample mean** (sample-mean): The average of the observations in a sample, used to estimate the true mean. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **sample standard deviation** (sample-standard-deviation): The square root of the sum of squared deviations divided by n − 1, used to estimate the true standard deviation. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **degrees of freedom** (degrees-of-freedom): The number of values that are free to vary when a statistic is computed. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **standard error** (standard-error): The standard deviation of an estimate, such as the sample mean, across different samples; it measures how precise the estimate is. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **central limit theorem** (central-limit-theorem): The average of many independent random variables is approximately normally distributed. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **confidence interval** (confidence-interval): An interval built from a sample by a method such that a stated share (for example 95%) of the intervals built this way contain the true parameter. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **t distribution** (t-distribution): The distribution used when the sample standard deviation replaces the true one; it has thicker tails than the normal distribution and approaches it as the sample grows. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **hypothesis test** (hypothesis-test): A method for deciding whether the data clearly contradict a hypothesis, such as a true mean of 0. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **t-statistic** (t-statistic): An estimate divided by its standard error: how many standard errors the estimate is from 0. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **statistical significance** (statistical-significance): If the null hypothesis were true, a result this extreme would occur with a probability below a chosen level, such as 5%. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **multiple testing** (multiple-testing): The problem of results that are significant by chance when many hypotheses are tested. (Defined in 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference)
- **regression** (regression): Describing how the average of one variable changes with another variable, with a line or another function. (Defined in 0.5 Regression)
- **ordinary least squares** (ols): The estimation method that chooses the intercept and slope to minimize the sum of squared residuals (OLS). (Defined in 0.5 Regression)
- **residual** (residual): The actual value minus the fitted value given by the regression line. (Defined in 0.5 Regression)
- **regression coefficient** (regression-coefficient): The number in front of an explanatory variable in a regression; the slope is the average change in the dependent variable per unit increase in the explanatory variable. (Defined in 0.5 Regression)
- **R-squared** (r-squared): The share of the variance of the dependent variable that the regression explains (R²), between 0 and 1. (Defined in 0.5 Regression)
- **omitted variable bias** (omitted-variable-bias): Bias in a coefficient estimate caused by leaving out a variable that affects the dependent variable and is correlated with an explanatory variable. (Defined in 0.5 Regression)
- **correlation and causation** (correlation-vs-causation): Two variables being correlated does not mean that one causes the other. (Defined in 0.5 Regression)
- **demand** (demand): The relation between the price of a good and the quantity that buyers are willing and able to buy, other things being equal. (Defined in 1.1 Supply and Demand)
- **supply** (supply): The relation between the price of a good and the quantity that sellers are willing and able to sell, other things being equal. (Defined in 1.1 Supply and Demand)
- **market equilibrium** (market-equilibrium): The price and quantity at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. (Defined in 1.1 Supply and Demand)
- **comparative statics** (comparative-statics): Comparing the equilibria before and after a change in an outside condition, without studying the path of adjustment. (Defined in 1.1 Supply and Demand)
- **price elasticity of demand** (price-elasticity): The percentage change in the quantity demanded when the price changes by 1%. (Defined in 1.1 Supply and Demand)
- **income elasticity** (income-elasticity): The percentage change in the quantity demanded when income changes by 1%. (Defined in 1.1 Supply and Demand)
- **cross-price elasticity** (cross-price-elasticity): The percentage change in the quantity demanded of a good when the price of another good changes by 1%. (Defined in 1.1 Supply and Demand)
- **preferences** (preferences): A consumer's ranking of different bundles of goods. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **utility function** (utility-function): A function that scores each bundle so that preferred bundles get higher scores; it is used only for ranking. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **marginal utility** (marginal-utility): The increase in utility from consuming one more unit of a good, other goods unchanged. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **indifference curve** (indifference-curve): The curve of all bundles that give the same utility. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **marginal rate of substitution** (marginal-rate-of-substitution): The quantity of y a consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of x; it equals MUx/MUy. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **substitution effect** (substitution-effect): The change in quantity demanded caused only by the change in relative prices, with purchasing power held constant. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **income effect** (income-effect): The change in quantity demanded caused by the change in real purchasing power when a price changes. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **Slutsky equation** (slutsky-equation): The equation that splits the effect of a price change on demand into a substitution effect and an income effect. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **Giffen good** (giffen-good): An inferior good whose income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so that the quantity demanded rises when its price rises. (Defined in 1.2 Consumer Theory)
- **intertemporal budget constraint** (intertemporal-budget-constraint): The present value of consumption over time equals the present value of income. (Defined in 1.3 Intertemporal Choice)
- **time preference** (time-preference): Valuing consumption now more than the same consumption in the future. (Defined in 1.3 Intertemporal Choice)
- **Euler equation** (euler-equation): The condition for the best consumption over time, u′(c₁) = β(1 + r)u′(c₂). (Defined in 1.3 Intertemporal Choice)
- **consumption smoothing** (consumption-smoothing): Using saving and borrowing to keep consumption steadier over time than income. (Defined in 1.3 Intertemporal Choice)
- **inflation rate** (inflation): The yearly growth rate of the general price level. (Defined in 1.3 Intertemporal Choice)
- **nominal interest rate** (nominal-interest-rate): The rate of return measured in money. (Defined in 1.3 Intertemporal Choice)
- **real interest rate** (real-interest-rate): The rate of return measured in purchasing power, about the nominal rate minus inflation. (Defined in 1.3 Intertemporal Choice)
- **Fisher equation** (fisher-equation): 1 + real rate = (1 + nominal rate) / (1 + inflation). (Defined in 1.3 Intertemporal Choice)
- **expected utility** (expected-utility): The probability-weighted average of the utility of each outcome. (Defined in 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty)
- **risk aversion** (risk-aversion): Preferring the expected value of a gamble for sure to the gamble itself; equivalent to a concave utility function. (Defined in 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty)
- **coefficient of absolute risk aversion** (absolute-risk-aversion): A(W) = −u″(W)/u′(W), which measures aversion to gambles of fixed dollar size. (Defined in 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty)
- **coefficient of relative risk aversion** (relative-risk-aversion): R(W) = −W u″(W)/u′(W), which measures aversion to gambles proportional to wealth. (Defined in 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty)
- **certainty equivalent** (certainty-equivalent): The sure amount that gives the same utility as the expected utility of a gamble. (Defined in 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty)
- **risk premium** (risk-premium): The expected value minus the certainty equivalent: the expected wealth one is willing to give up to remove the risk. (Defined in 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty)
- **CRRA utility** (crra-utility): The utility function W^(1−γ)/(1−γ) with constant relative risk aversion γ; ln W when γ = 1. (Defined in 1.4 Choice Under Uncertainty)
- **production function** (production-function): The relation Q = f(K, L) between inputs (capital K, labor L) and the maximum output. (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **short run** (short-run): A period in which at least one input (usually capital) cannot be adjusted. (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **long run** (long-run): A period in which all inputs can be adjusted and firms can enter or exit the industry. (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **marginal product** (marginal-product): The extra output from one more unit of an input with the other inputs fixed, such as MP_L = ∂Q/∂L. (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **returns to scale** (returns-to-scale): Whether output rises by more than, exactly or less than t times when all inputs rise t times (increasing, constant, decreasing). (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **average cost** (average-cost): Cost divided by output: average variable cost AVC = VC/q and average total cost ATC = C/q. (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **perfect competition** (perfect-competition): A market with many firms, identical products and free entry and exit, where every firm takes the market price as given. (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **shutdown point** (shutdown-point): The minimum of AVC; below this price a firm does better by shutting down in the short run. (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **economic profit** (economic-profit): Revenue minus all costs including opportunity costs; when it is 0 the inputs earn a normal return. (Defined in 1.5 Producer Theory)
- **monopoly** (monopoly): A market with a single seller of a product without close substitutes; it sets output where MR = MC and reads the price from the demand curve. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **Lerner index** (lerner-index): (P − MC)/P, the share of the price above marginal cost; at the profit maximum it equals 1/|ε| and measures market power. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **price discrimination** (price-discrimination): Charging different buyers different prices that do not reflect cost differences; first, second or third degree. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **oligopoly** (oligopoly): A market with only a few firms whose decisions affect each other. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **Cournot model** (cournot-model): An oligopoly model in which firms choose quantities simultaneously; equilibrium output lies between monopoly and perfect competition. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **Bertrand model** (bertrand-model): An oligopoly model in which firms choose prices simultaneously; with identical products and costs, two firms already drive the price to marginal cost. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **monopolistic competition** (monopolistic-competition): A market with many firms, differentiated products and free entry; economic profit is 0 in the long run. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **barriers to entry** (barriers-to-entry): Factors that keep new firms from entering or imitating: economies of scale, network effects, switching costs, intangible assets, cost advantages. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **natural monopoly** (natural-monopoly): An industry in which average cost falls over the whole range of market demand, so one firm can produce at the lowest cost. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **economic moat** (economic-moat): A durable competitive advantage that keeps a firm's economic profit positive for a long time. (Defined in 1.6 Market Structure)
- **game** (game): A situation in which the payoffs of several decision makers depend on each other's choices; it consists of players, strategies and payoffs. (Defined in 1.7 Basic Game Theory)
- **dominant strategy** (dominant-strategy): A strategy that is better than the player's other strategies whatever the others choose. (Defined in 1.7 Basic Game Theory)
- **prisoner's dilemma** (prisoners-dilemma): A game in which each player's dominant strategy leads to an outcome that is worse for everyone than another outcome. (Defined in 1.7 Basic Game Theory)
- **Nash equilibrium** (nash-equilibrium): A combination of strategies in which each player's strategy is a best response to the others', so no one wants to change alone. (Defined in 1.7 Basic Game Theory)
- **backward induction** (backward-induction): Solving a sequential game by finding the best choice at the last decision first and then working back step by step. (Defined in 1.7 Basic Game Theory)
- **repeated game** (repeated-game): The same game played period after period; today's choice affects the other side's later choices, so cooperation may be sustained. (Defined in 1.7 Basic Game Theory)
- **consumer surplus** (consumer-surplus): The sum of buyers' willingness to pay minus the price they actually pay: the area below the demand curve and above the price. (Defined in 1.8 Welfare and Market Failure)
- **producer surplus** (producer-surplus): The sum of the price sellers receive minus marginal cost: the area below the price and above the supply curve, equal to revenue minus variable cost. (Defined in 1.8 Welfare and Market Failure)
- **deadweight loss** (deadweight-loss): The part of total surplus that no one gets when the quantity traded differs from the efficient quantity. (Defined in 1.8 Welfare and Market Failure)
- **tax incidence** (tax-incidence): How the burden of a tax is actually split between buyers and sellers. (Defined in 1.8 Welfare and Market Failure)
- **externality** (externality): An effect of one party's decision on others that is not reflected in prices. (Defined in 1.8 Welfare and Market Failure)
- **Pigouvian tax** (pigouvian-tax): A tax per unit equal to its external cost, which makes the decision maker face the full social cost. (Defined in 1.8 Welfare and Market Failure)
- **public good** (public-good): A good that is neither rival nor excludable; it has a free-rider problem, and markets provide too little of it. (Defined in 1.8 Welfare and Market Failure)
- **asymmetric information** (asymmetric-information): One side of a transaction knows something the other side does not. (Defined in 1.9 Information Economics)
- **adverse selection** (adverse-selection): Hidden information before a transaction leaves the less-informed side facing the worst counterparties, as the good types leave the market. (Defined in 1.9 Information Economics)
- **signaling** (signaling): The better-informed side reveals its type through an action that is cheap for good types and expensive for bad types. (Defined in 1.9 Information Economics)
- **screening** (screening): The less-informed side designs a set of choices so that the other side reveals its type by what it chooses. (Defined in 1.9 Information Economics)
- **moral hazard** (moral-hazard): A contract that relieves one side of the full consequences of its actions changes those actions, which the other side cannot see. (Defined in 1.9 Information Economics)
- **principal-agent problem** (principal-agent-problem): An agent acts for a principal, but their interests differ and the principal cannot fully observe the agent's actions. (Defined in 1.9 Information Economics)
- **gross domestic product** (gdp): The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a period. (Defined in 2.1 Macroeconomic Data)
- **real GDP** (real-gdp): GDP valued at the prices of a fixed base year, so that it reflects only changes in output. (Defined in 2.1 Macroeconomic Data)
- **GDP deflator** (gdp-deflator): Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100; a measure of the price level of all goods and services produced at home. (Defined in 2.1 Macroeconomic Data)
- **consumer price index** (cpi): The price level of a fixed basket of consumer goods and services, published monthly by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. (Defined in 2.1 Macroeconomic Data)
- **PCE price index** (pce-price-index): The personal consumption expenditures price index: broader than the CPI, with weights updated each period; the Fed defines its inflation target with it. (Defined in 2.1 Macroeconomic Data)
- **core inflation** (core-inflation): Inflation excluding the volatile prices of food and energy. (Defined in 2.1 Macroeconomic Data)
- **unemployment rate** (unemployment-rate): The unemployed as a share of the labor force; the unemployed are people without a job who are available and looking for work. (Defined in 2.1 Macroeconomic Data)
- **labor force participation rate** (labor-force-participation-rate): The labor force (employed plus unemployed) as a share of the population aged 16 and over. (Defined in 2.1 Macroeconomic Data)
- **total factor productivity** (total-factor-productivity): The $A$ in the production function: how much the same capital and labor can produce, including technology, organization and institutions. (Defined in 2.2 Long-Run Growth)
- **growth accounting** (growth-accounting): Splitting output growth into the contributions of capital, labor and TFP: $g_Y = g_A + \alpha g_K + (1 - \alpha) g_L$. (Defined in 2.2 Long-Run Growth)
- **Solow model** (solow-model): A growth model of capital accumulation: the change in capital per worker is investment per worker minus the investment needed to keep capital per worker constant. (Defined in 2.2 Long-Run Growth)
- **steady state** (steady-state): The state in which investment just equals what is needed, so capital per worker no longer changes. (Defined in 2.2 Long-Run Growth)
- **money supply** (money-supply): The total amount of money in the economy, including currency and bank deposits, often measured by M2. (Defined in 2.3 Money and Banking)
- **monetary base** (monetary-base): Currency in circulation plus banks' reserves at the central bank; directly controlled by the central bank. (Defined in 2.3 Money and Banking)
- **fractional reserve banking** (fractional-reserve-banking): Banks keep only part of their deposits as reserves and lend the rest, so loans create new deposits. (Defined in 2.3 Money and Banking)
- **money multiplier** (money-multiplier): The ratio of the money supply to the monetary base, $m = \frac{1 + c}{c + r}$. (Defined in 2.3 Money and Banking)
- **bank run** (bank-run): Depositors rushing to withdraw because they fear the bank will fail; it can be self-fulfilling. (Defined in 2.3 Money and Banking)
- **deposit insurance** (deposit-insurance): A government guarantee of deposits up to a limit if a bank fails; it prevents runs but brings moral hazard. (Defined in 2.3 Money and Banking)
- **quantity theory of money** (quantity-theory-of-money): From $MV = PY$, assuming stable velocity and output independent of money, the theory that in the long run money growth mainly brings inflation. (Defined in 2.3 Money and Banking)
- **potential output** (potential-output): The output produced when all resources are used at normal rates, determined by capital, labor and TFP. (Defined in 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations)
- **output gap** (output-gap): Actual minus potential output as a share of potential output, $\frac{Y - Y^*}{Y^*}$. (Defined in 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations)
- **IS curve** (is-curve): The relation between the real interest rate and the output at which output equals planned spending; a higher rate means less investment and lower output. (Defined in 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations)
- **aggregate demand** (aggregate-demand): The total quantity of output demanded in the economy at each price level; the AD curve slopes down. (Defined in 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations)
- **aggregate supply** (aggregate-supply): The output firms are willing to produce at each price level; upward-sloping in the short run, vertical at potential output in the long run. (Defined in 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations)
- **natural rate of unemployment** (natural-rate-of-unemployment): The normal unemployment rate when the economy is neither in recession nor overheating. (Defined in 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations)
- **Phillips curve** (phillips-curve): The relation between inflation and unemployment: $\pi = \pi^e - \beta(u - u^*)$. (Defined in 2.4 Short-Run Fluctuations)
- **federal funds rate** (federal-funds-rate): The rate at which US banks lend reserves to each other overnight; the FOMC sets a target range for it. (Defined in 2.5 Monetary Policy)
- **zero lower bound** (zero-lower-bound): Nominal interest rates cannot go far below zero, because people can hold cash instead. (Defined in 2.5 Monetary Policy)
- **quantitative easing** (quantitative-easing): Large central bank purchases of long-term bonds to push long-term rates down directly. (Defined in 2.5 Monetary Policy)
- **forward guidance** (forward-guidance): Central bank statements about the future path of rates, which affect long rates by changing expected future short rates. (Defined in 2.5 Monetary Policy)
- **Taylor rule** (taylor-rule): A reference rule setting the policy rate from inflation and the output gap: $i = r^* + \pi + 0.5(\pi - \pi^T) + 0.5\,\text{gap}$. (Defined in 2.5 Monetary Policy)
- **neutral interest rate** (neutral-interest-rate): The real interest rate $r^*$ that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy; it can only be estimated. (Defined in 2.5 Monetary Policy)
- **budget deficit** (budget-deficit): The amount by which government spending exceeds revenue, financed by borrowing. (Defined in 2.6 Fiscal Policy)
- **primary deficit** (primary-deficit): The budget deficit excluding interest payments. (Defined in 2.6 Fiscal Policy)
- **fiscal multiplier** (fiscal-multiplier): The change in output divided by the change in government spending or taxes. (Defined in 2.6 Fiscal Policy)
- **automatic stabilizer** (automatic-stabilizer): Taxes and spending that move against the cycle automatically, such as income taxes and unemployment benefits. (Defined in 2.6 Fiscal Policy)
- **crowding out** (crowding-out): Government borrowing for spending that raises interest rates and reduces private investment. (Defined in 2.6 Fiscal Policy)
- **Ricardian equivalence** (ricardian-equivalence): Given government spending, financing by taxes or by debt has the same effect, because rational households save a tax cut to pay future taxes. (Defined in 2.6 Fiscal Policy)
- **current account** (current-account): Net exports plus net investment income and net transfers from abroad; a deficit matches an equal net capital inflow. (Defined in 2.7 The Open Economy)
- **nominal exchange rate** (nominal-exchange-rate): The rate at which two currencies exchange; in this course, the home-currency price of one unit of foreign currency. (Defined in 2.7 The Open Economy)
- **real exchange rate** (real-exchange-rate): The exchange rate adjusted for price levels, $\varepsilon = \frac{EP^*}{P}$, comparing the relative prices of two countries' goods. (Defined in 2.7 The Open Economy)
- **purchasing power parity** (purchasing-power-parity): Exchange rates that equalize the purchasing power of two currencies; in relative form, $\frac{\Delta E}{E} \approx \pi - \pi^*$. (Defined in 2.7 The Open Economy)
- **covered interest parity** (covered-interest-parity): $\frac{F}{E} = \frac{1 + i}{1 + i^*}$: after hedging with a forward contract, a foreign investment earns the home interest rate. (Defined in 2.7 The Open Economy)
- **uncovered interest parity** (uncovered-interest-parity): The expected depreciation of a high-rate currency is about the interest differential; it often fails in the short run. (Defined in 2.7 The Open Economy)
- **currency hedging** (currency-hedging): Removing the currency risk of a foreign investment with forward contracts or similar tools; it costs about the interest differential. (Defined in 2.7 The Open Economy)
- **business cycle** (business-cycle): The expansions and contractions of output around its potential, with no fixed length. (Defined in 2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices)
- **recession** (recession): A significant, widespread decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months; dated in the US by the NBER. (Defined in 2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices)
- **leading indicator** (leading-indicator): An indicator that usually changes before turning points in the economy, such as housing permits, jobless claims and stock prices. (Defined in 2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices)
- **yield curve** (yield-curve): The curve of government bond yields across maturities; when long rates are below short rates it is inverted. (Defined in 2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices)
- **stock-bond correlation** (stock-bond-correlation): The correlation between stock and bond returns; negative when demand shocks dominate, positive when inflation shocks dominate. (Defined in 2.8 Business Cycles and Asset Prices)
- **financial intermediary** (financial-intermediary): An institution that channels funds from savers to borrowers, such as a bank, an insurer or a fund. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **money market** (money-market): The market for short-term debt of up to a year, such as Treasury bills, commercial paper and repos. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **capital market** (capital-market): The market for debt with maturities over a year and for stocks. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **primary market** (primary-market): The market where securities are first issued and money flows from investors to the issuer. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **secondary market** (secondary-market): The market where investors trade securities already issued; it provides liquidity and prices. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **market maker** (market-maker): A firm that continuously quotes bid and ask prices and stands ready to trade. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **bid-ask spread** (bid-ask-spread): The ask price minus the bid price; the cost of trading immediately. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **short selling** (short-selling): Selling borrowed shares and buying them back later; it gains when the price falls and has unlimited potential loss. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **limit order** (limit-order): An order that trades only at a stated price or better; the price is guaranteed, execution is not. (Defined in 3.1 Overview of the Financial System)
- **net present value** (net-present-value): The sum of all of a project's cash flows discounted at the cost of capital; if positive, the project adds to shareholder wealth. (Defined in 3.2 NPV, IRR and Capital Budgeting)
- **cost of capital** (cost-of-capital): The expected return on investments of the same risk; the opportunity cost used as a project's discount rate. (Defined in 3.2 NPV, IRR and Capital Budgeting)
- **internal rate of return** (internal-rate-of-return): The discount rate at which a project's NPV is zero. (Defined in 3.2 NPV, IRR and Capital Budgeting)
- **payback period** (payback-period): The time for cumulative cash flows to recover the initial investment; it ignores time value and later cash flows. (Defined in 3.2 NPV, IRR and Capital Budgeting)
- **profitability index** (profitability-index): NPV divided by the initial investment, used to rank projects under capital rationing. (Defined in 3.2 NPV, IRR and Capital Budgeting)
- **coupon rate** (coupon-rate): The yearly coupon divided by the face value. (Defined in 3.3 Bond Pricing)
- **yield to maturity** (yield-to-maturity): The discount rate that makes the present value of a bond's cash flows equal its market price: the IRR of buying at that price. (Defined in 3.3 Bond Pricing)
- **zero-coupon bond** (zero-coupon-bond): A bond that pays only its face value at maturity, with no coupons. (Defined in 3.3 Bond Pricing)
- **spot rate** (spot-rate): The yield on a t-year zero-coupon bond; each cash flow should be discounted at the spot rate for its own maturity. (Defined in 3.3 Bond Pricing)
- **forward rate** (forward-rate): The rate for a future period implied by spot rates and lockable today: $(1 + s_2)^2 = (1 + s_1)(1 + f_{1,2})$. (Defined in 3.3 Bond Pricing)
- **Macaulay duration** (macaulay-duration): The average time to receive cash, weighted by present value, $D = \sum_t t\,w_t$; a zero's duration equals its maturity. (Defined in 3.4 Interest Rate Risk)
- **modified duration** (modified-duration): $D^* = \frac{D}{1 + y}$; a 1-point change in yield moves the price about $D^*$ percent in the opposite direction. (Defined in 3.4 Interest Rate Risk)
- **convexity** (convexity): The curvature of the price–yield curve, correcting the duration estimate: $\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \Delta y + \frac{1}{2} C (\Delta y)^2$. (Defined in 3.4 Interest Rate Risk)
- **immunization** (immunization): Matching the present values and durations of assets and liabilities so that the price and reinvestment effects of a rate change offset. (Defined in 3.4 Interest Rate Risk)
- **term structure of interest rates** (term-structure): The relation between interest rates and maturity for one issuer, shown by the yield curve. (Defined in 3.5 The Term Structure of Interest Rates)
- **expectations hypothesis** (expectations-hypothesis): Long rates are the geometric average of expected future short rates; forward rates equal expected future short rates. (Defined in 3.5 The Term Structure of Interest Rates)
- **term premium** (term-premium): The amount by which forward rates (or long rates) exceed expected future short rates, compensating for the risk of long bonds; it can be positive or negative. (Defined in 3.5 The Term Structure of Interest Rates)
- **preferred habitat theory** (preferred-habitat): Investors prefer maturities that fit their needs, so supply and demand at each maturity affect the term premium. (Defined in 3.5 The Term Structure of Interest Rates)
- **default risk** (default-risk): The risk that a borrower fails to pay interest or principal as promised. (Defined in 3.6 Credit Risk)
- **recovery rate** (recovery-rate): The share of face value that creditors finally recover after a default. (Defined in 3.6 Credit Risk)
- **credit spread** (credit-spread): The amount by which the yield of a bond with default risk exceeds the yield of a Treasury of the same maturity. (Defined in 3.6 Credit Risk)
- **credit rating** (credit-rating): A rating agency's grade of the default risk of an issuer or a bond; BBB− (Baa3) and above is investment grade. (Defined in 3.6 Credit Risk)
- **municipal bond** (municipal-bond): A bond issued by a US state or local government; its interest is usually exempt from federal income tax. (Defined in 3.6 Credit Risk)
- **tax-equivalent yield** (tax-equivalent-yield): The yield a taxable bond needs to match a tax-exempt bond after tax: the tax-exempt yield divided by one minus the marginal tax rate. (Defined in 3.6 Credit Risk)
- **TIPS** (tips): US Treasury securities whose principal is adjusted by the CPI; their yield is a real yield. (Defined in 3.6 Credit Risk)
- **breakeven inflation** (breakeven-inflation): The inflation rate at which a nominal Treasury and a TIPS of the same maturity give the same return, roughly the difference in their yields. (Defined in 3.6 Credit Risk)
- **balance sheet** (balance-sheet): A company's assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity at a point in time; assets = liabilities + equity. (Defined in 3.7 Financial Statement Analysis)
- **income statement** (income-statement): Revenue, expenses and net income over a period. (Defined in 3.7 Financial Statement Analysis)
- **cash flow statement** (cash-flow-statement): Cash received and paid over a period, split into operating, investing and financing activities. (Defined in 3.7 Financial Statement Analysis)
- **accrual accounting** (accrual-accounting): Revenue is recognized when goods or services are delivered and expenses in the period of the related revenue, regardless of when cash moves. (Defined in 3.7 Financial Statement Analysis)
- **depreciation** (depreciation): Spreading the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life as an expense in each period; it is not a cash payment in that period. (Defined in 3.7 Financial Statement Analysis)
- **working capital** (working-capital): Money tied up in daily operations, mainly receivables plus inventory minus payables. (Defined in 3.7 Financial Statement Analysis)
- **earnings quality** (earnings-quality): How far reported earnings reflect lasting results of the business that turn into cash. (Defined in 3.7 Financial Statement Analysis)
- **return on assets** (return-on-assets): Profit divided by total assets, measuring how much profit the assets earn; ROA. (Defined in 3.8 Financial Ratios)
- **return on equity** (return-on-equity): Net income divided by shareholders' equity, the return on shareholders' book capital; ROE. (Defined in 3.8 Financial Ratios)
- **DuPont analysis** (dupont-analysis): Splitting ROE into net margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier. (Defined in 3.8 Financial Ratios)
- **financial leverage** (financial-leverage): Financing assets with debt; it raises ROE when the return on assets exceeds the interest rate, lowers it otherwise, and makes ROE more volatile. (Defined in 3.8 Financial Ratios)
- **return on invested capital** (return-on-invested-capital): After-tax operating profit divided by invested capital (equity plus interest-bearing debt), independent of financing; ROIC. (Defined in 3.8 Financial Ratios)
- **interest coverage** (interest-coverage): Operating income (EBIT) divided by interest expense. (Defined in 3.8 Financial Ratios)
- **current ratio** (current-ratio): Current assets divided by current liabilities, a measure of the ability to pay short-term obligations. (Defined in 3.8 Financial Ratios)
- **dividend discount model** (dividend-discount-model): A stock's intrinsic value equals the present value of expected future dividends, discounted at the cost of equity; DDM. (Defined in 3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models)
- **cost of equity** (cost-of-equity): The expected return shareholders require given the stock's risk, used to discount cash flows to shareholders. (Defined in 3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models)
- **Gordon growth model** (gordon-growth-model): If dividends grow forever at a constant g, the price is P0 = D1 / (r − g), which requires g < r. (Defined in 3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models)
- **payout ratio** (payout-ratio): Dividends as a share of net income; one minus the payout ratio is the retention ratio. (Defined in 3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models)
- **sustainable growth rate** (sustainable-growth-rate): The growth rate reachable by retaining profit without more leverage or new shares: g = retention ratio × ROE. (Defined in 3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models)
- **present value of growth opportunities** (pvgo): The part of the price above the no-growth value E1 / r; PVGO. (Defined in 3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models)
- **free cash flow to the firm** (fcff): Cash available to all investors (shareholders and creditors) after necessary investment: EBIT(1 − t) + depreciation − capital spending − increase in working capital; FCFF. (Defined in 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow)
- **free cash flow to equity** (fcfe): Cash available to shareholders after after-tax interest and net borrowing; FCFE. (Defined in 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow)
- **weighted average cost of capital** (wacc): The cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt weighted by market values, used to discount FCFF; WACC. (Defined in 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow)
- **interest tax shield** (interest-tax-shield): The tax saved because interest is deductible; roughly interest times the tax rate each year. (Defined in 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow)
- **terminal value** (terminal-value): The value at the end of the forecast period of all later cash flows, often computed as a growing perpetuity. (Defined in 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow)
- **enterprise value** (enterprise-value): The value of the operating business to all investors; equity value = enterprise value − net debt. (Defined in 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow)
- **price-earnings ratio** (price-earnings-ratio): Price divided by earnings per share (P/E); trailing if based on the last 12 months of earnings, forward if based on forecast earnings. (Defined in 3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation)
- **EV/EBITDA** (ev-ebitda): Enterprise value divided by EBITDA, unaffected by capital structure and depreciation policy. (Defined in 3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation)
- **price-to-book ratio** (price-to-book): Price divided by book equity per share (P/B). (Defined in 3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation)
- **price-to-sales ratio** (price-to-sales): Market value of equity divided by revenue (P/S), usable for companies with negative or unstable profit, but only together with margins. (Defined in 3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation)
- **cyclically adjusted P/E** (cape): Price divided by average inflation-adjusted earnings of the past 10 years; CAPE, also called the Shiller P/E. (Defined in 3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation)
- **arithmetic mean return** (arithmetic-mean-return): The simple average of period returns, an estimate of the expected return for the next period. (Defined in 4.1 Measuring Return and Risk)
- **geometric mean return** (geometric-mean-return): The per-period rate that, compounded, gives the same final wealth: the compound annual growth rate. (Defined in 4.1 Measuring Return and Risk)
- **volatility drag** (volatility-drag): Volatility makes the geometric mean return lower than the arithmetic mean, by about half the variance: G ≈ μ − σ²/2. (Defined in 4.1 Measuring Return and Risk)
- **annualized volatility** (annualized-volatility): The standard deviation of returns scaled to one year; with independent periods, the per-period standard deviation times the square root of periods per year. (Defined in 4.1 Measuring Return and Risk)
- **maximum drawdown** (maximum-drawdown): The largest fall in wealth from a previous peak to a later trough over a period. (Defined in 4.1 Measuring Return and Risk)
- **Sharpe ratio** (sharpe-ratio): Excess return (return minus the risk-free rate) divided by the standard deviation of returns: excess return per unit of volatility. (Defined in 4.1 Measuring Return and Risk)
- **equity premium** (equity-premium): The amount by which the expected return on stocks exceeds the return on a riskless asset. (Defined in 4.1 Measuring Return and Risk)
- **minimum-variance portfolio** (minimum-variance-portfolio): The portfolio with the lowest variance among all possible portfolios. (Defined in 4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory)
- **minimum-variance frontier** (minimum-variance-frontier): The curve of portfolios with the lowest variance for each target expected return. (Defined in 4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory)
- **efficient frontier** (efficient-frontier): The part of the minimum-variance frontier above the minimum-variance portfolio: the portfolios with the highest expected return for their risk. (Defined in 4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory)
- **mean–variance optimization** (mean-variance-optimization): Choosing weights to minimize portfolio variance for a given expected return (or maximize expected return for a given variance), proposed by Markowitz. (Defined in 4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory)
- **short-sale constraint** (short-sale-constraint): The constraint that every weight be at least 0; it can put the optimum on the boundary. (Defined in 4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory)
- **capital allocation line** (capital-allocation-line): The straight line of combinations of a risky portfolio with the risk-free asset; its slope is the risky portfolio's Sharpe ratio; CAL. (Defined in 4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line)
- **tangency portfolio** (tangency-portfolio): The risky portfolio where the capital allocation line touches the efficient frontier: the risky portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio, also called the optimal risky portfolio. (Defined in 4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line)
- **separation theorem** (separation-theorem): Choosing the risky portfolio and deciding how much to put in it are separate: every investor holds the same tangency portfolio and uses risk aversion only to decide how much. (Defined in 4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line)
- **mean–variance utility** (mean-variance-utility): U = E[r] − ½γσ², valuing a portfolio by its expected return minus a cost for risk; γ is the risk-aversion coefficient. (Defined in 4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line)
- **market portfolio** (market-portfolio): The portfolio of all risky assets weighted by market value. (Defined in 4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line)
- **capital market line** (capital-market-line): The capital allocation line whose risky portfolio is the market portfolio; CML. (Defined in 4.3 The Capital Allocation Line and the Capital Market Line)
- **capital asset pricing model** (capm): In equilibrium, an asset's expected excess return is proportional to its beta: E[R_i] − r_f = β_i(E[R_M] − r_f); CAPM. (Defined in 4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM))
- **beta** (beta): The covariance of an asset's return with the market return divided by the market return's variance: how sensitive the asset is to market moves. (Defined in 4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM))
- **security market line** (security-market-line): The straight line the CAPM gives with beta on the horizontal axis and expected return on the vertical axis; SML. (Defined in 4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM))
- **alpha** (alpha): The amount by which an asset's expected (or realized) return exceeds the return the security market line requires. (Defined in 4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM))
- **single-index model** (single-index-model): Assumes that the only link between stock returns is a common market index: R_i − r_f = α_i + β_i(R_M − r_f) + e_i, with residuals uncorrelated across companies. (Defined in 4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta)
- **systematic risk** (systematic-risk): Risk that moves with the market and cannot be removed by diversification; β_i²σ_M² in the single-index model. (Defined in 4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta)
- **firm-specific risk** (firm-specific-risk): Risk that concerns only the company itself and is unrelated to the market; it can be diversified away; σ²(e_i) in the single-index model. (Defined in 4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta)
- **adjusted beta** (adjusted-beta): A regression beta shrunk toward 1 (or another reference value), commonly (2/3)β̂ + 1/3, to reduce estimation error. (Defined in 4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta)
- **multifactor model** (multifactor-model): A model that describes asset returns with several common factors: R_i − r_f = α_i + Σ β_ik F_k + e_i. (Defined in 4.6 Multifactor Models)
- **factor loading** (factor-loading): How sensitive an asset's return is to a factor: the factor's coefficient in a multifactor model; also called a factor beta. (Defined in 4.6 Multifactor Models)
- **arbitrage** (arbitrage): A trade that costs nothing, has no risk and has a positive return. (Defined in 4.6 Multifactor Models)
- **arbitrage pricing theory** (arbitrage-pricing-theory): Under a multifactor model and no arbitrage, the expected excess return equals the sum of the factor loadings times the factor risk premia; APT. (Defined in 4.6 Multifactor Models)
- **factor risk premium** (factor-risk-premium): The expected excess return of a portfolio with a loading of 1 on one factor and 0 on the others. (Defined in 4.6 Multifactor Models)
- **Fama–French three-factor model** (fama-french-model): A model that describes stock returns with three factors: the market, size (SMB) and value (HML); the five-factor model adds profitability and investment factors. (Defined in 4.6 Multifactor Models)
- **momentum** (momentum): The tendency of stocks that rose most over the past 3 to 12 months to keep beating those that fell most over the next few months. (Defined in 4.6 Multifactor Models)
- **smart beta** (smart-beta): Rule-based index funds tilted toward some factors (value, small size, momentum and so on); also called factor investing. (Defined in 4.6 Multifactor Models)
- **efficient market hypothesis** (efficient-market-hypothesis): Prices fully reflect available information, so apart from the average return risk requires, price changes cannot be predicted; EMH. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **random walk** (random-walk): Price changes are unpredictable; past changes do not predict future ones. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **weak-form efficiency** (weak-form-efficiency): Prices reflect past prices and trading volume, so technical analysis cannot earn excess returns. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **semi-strong-form efficiency** (semi-strong-form-efficiency): Prices reflect all public information, so analyzing public information cannot earn excess returns. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **strong-form efficiency** (strong-form-efficiency): Prices reflect all information, including nonpublic inside information. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **joint hypothesis problem** (joint-hypothesis-problem): Testing market efficiency requires assuming a model of expected returns as well, so beating the model may mean either inefficiency or a wrong model. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **event study** (event-study): A method that uses abnormal and cumulative abnormal returns around events to test how prices react to a kind of news. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **abnormal return** (abnormal-return): The actual return minus the normal return given by a model such as the single-index model. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **market anomaly** (market-anomaly): A pattern in returns that can be predicted from public information and does not fit the asset pricing model. (Defined in 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis)
- **prospect theory** (prospect-theory): A theory of how people actually choose under risk: gains and losses judged relative to a reference point, loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity and overweighting of small probabilities. (Defined in 4.8 Behavioral Finance)
- **loss aversion** (loss-aversion): A loss hurts more than a gain of the same size pleases, by a factor of a little more than two. (Defined in 4.8 Behavioral Finance)
- **overconfidence** (overconfidence): Overrating the accuracy of one's own knowledge and judgment, which often leads to trading too much. (Defined in 4.8 Behavioral Finance)
- **disposition effect** (disposition-effect): A tendency to sell winning stocks too early and hold losing stocks too long. (Defined in 4.8 Behavioral Finance)
- **mental accounting** (mental-accounting): Putting money into separate "accounts" and treating each on its own, ignoring that money is interchangeable. (Defined in 4.8 Behavioral Finance)
- **herding** (herding): Following what others do instead of judging from one's own information. (Defined in 4.8 Behavioral Finance)
- **limits to arbitrage** (limits-to-arbitrage): Fundamental risk, noise trader risk, implementation costs and funding make arbitrage risky and costly, so mispricing can persist. (Defined in 4.8 Behavioral Finance)
- **noise trader risk** (noise-trader-risk): The risk that the investors pushing prices away from value become more extreme in the short run, so the gap widens before it narrows. (Defined in 4.8 Behavioral Finance)
- **Treynor ratio** (treynor-ratio): Excess return divided by beta: the excess return per unit of systematic risk. (Defined in 4.9 Performance Evaluation)
- **Jensen's alpha** (jensens-alpha): The amount by which the actual average return exceeds the return the security market line requires, usually estimated by a regression intercept. (Defined in 4.9 Performance Evaluation)
- **information ratio** (information-ratio): Alpha divided by the residual standard deviation (or the average return over a benchmark divided by the tracking error). (Defined in 4.9 Performance Evaluation)
- **tracking error** (tracking-error): The standard deviation of the difference between a portfolio's return and its benchmark's. (Defined in 4.9 Performance Evaluation)
- **survivorship bias** (survivorship-bias): Overstating performance by computing it only from funds (or companies) that survived, ignoring those that were closed or merged. (Defined in 4.9 Performance Evaluation)
- **error maximization** (error-maximization): The tendency of a mean–variance optimizer to favor assets with favorable estimation errors, magnifying those errors. (Defined in 4.10 Estimation Error and Robust Optimization)
- **out of sample** (out-of-sample): Testing results on data that were not used to estimate or choose the model. (Defined in 4.10 Estimation Error and Robust Optimization)
- **shrinkage estimator** (shrinkage-estimator): An estimator that pulls individual estimates toward a common reference value, accepting some bias for less variable errors. (Defined in 4.10 Estimation Error and Robust Optimization)
- **resampling** (resampling): A method that generates many sets of inputs according to the estimation errors, optimizes each and averages the weights. (Defined in 4.10 Estimation Error and Robust Optimization)
- **capital market assumptions** (capital-market-assumptions): A set of assumptions about asset classes' future expected returns, volatilities and correlations, used for asset allocation and planning. (Defined in 4.11 Capital Market Assumptions)
- **building-block approach** (building-block-approach): Estimating expected stock returns as shareholder yield plus real earnings growth plus inflation plus valuation change; bonds by their starting yield. (Defined in 4.11 Capital Market Assumptions)
- **reverse optimization** (reverse-optimization): Assuming the market portfolio is optimal, working back from market weights and covariances to implied expected returns: Π = δΣw. (Defined in 4.11 Capital Market Assumptions)
- **Black–Litterman model** (black-litterman): A model that starts from equilibrium returns from reverse optimization and adds investor views according to confidence, giving weighted-average expected returns. (Defined in 4.11 Capital Market Assumptions)
- **Merton share** (merton-share): The optimal risky share of a CRRA investor with constant investment opportunities, (μ − r_f)/(γσ²), independent of wealth and horizon. (Defined in 4.12 Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory)
- **human capital** (human-capital): The present value of future labor income; stable income is bond-like, income tied to the stock market is stock-like. (Defined in 4.12 Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory)
- **target-date fund** (target-date-fund): A fund that lowers its stock share automatically toward a planned retirement year. (Defined in 4.12 Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory)
- **glide path** (glide-path): The curve of the stock share against age (or years to retirement). (Defined in 4.12 Life-Cycle Asset Allocation Theory)
- **Monte Carlo simulation** (monte-carlo-simulation): A method that generates many random paths from an assumed distribution and tallies the distribution of outcomes. (Defined in 4.13 Simulation and Backtesting Methods)
- **bootstrap** (bootstrap): Simulating by drawing at random with replacement from historical data, keeping the shape of the historical distribution (such as fat tails). (Defined in 4.13 Simulation and Backtesting Methods)
- **backtest** (backtest): Computing, on historical data, what a strategy's rules would have produced if followed in the past. (Defined in 4.13 Simulation and Backtesting Methods)
- **look-ahead bias** (look-ahead-bias): Bias from using, in a backtest, information that was not available at the time. (Defined in 4.13 Simulation and Backtesting Methods)
- **overfitting** (overfitting): Trying many rules or parameters on the same data and picking the best, so the result fits the noise in the data. (Defined in 4.13 Simulation and Backtesting Methods)
- **forward contract** (forward-contract): A contract in which two parties agree today to trade an asset at a future date at a price fixed today. (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **derivative** (derivative-security): A financial contract whose value depends on the price of another asset (the underlying), such as forwards, futures, options and swaps. (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **cost-of-carry model** (cost-of-carry): Without arbitrage, the forward price equals the spot price plus the net cost of holding the asset to maturity: F = S₀e^{(r − q)T}. (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **contango** (contango): A market in which forward or futures prices are above the spot price; below the spot price is called backwardation. (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **futures contract** (futures-contract): A standardized forward contract traded on an exchange, guaranteed by a clearinghouse and settled daily at market prices. (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **margin** (margin): Collateral deposited to trade futures (or to buy securities on credit); it must be topped up when it falls below the maintenance level. (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **mark-to-market** (mark-to-market): Settling gains and losses at market prices every day, crediting them to the margin account at once. (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **hedging** (hedging): Using derivatives or other positions to offset an existing risk, reducing the uncertainty of outcomes. (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **basis** (basis): The spot price minus the futures price; changes in the basis make hedges imperfect (basis risk). (Defined in 5.1 Forwards and Futures)
- **call option** (call-option): The right to buy the underlying at the strike price on (or before) expiry; payoff max(S_T − K, 0). (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **put option** (put-option): The right to sell the underlying at the strike price on (or before) expiry; payoff max(K − S_T, 0). (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **strike price** (strike-price): The price at which an option lets its holder buy or sell the underlying. (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **option premium** (option-premium): The price the option buyer pays the writer for the option. (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **intrinsic value** (intrinsic-value): What an option would bring if exercised immediately; max(S − K, 0) for a call. (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **time value** (time-value): The part of an option's price above its intrinsic value, coming from the asymmetry of payoffs before expiry. (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **protective put** (protective-put): Holding a stock and buying a put on it, capping the worst outcome. (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **covered call** (covered-call): Holding a stock and selling a call on it, collecting the premium and giving up gains above the strike. (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **employee stock option** (employee-stock-option): A long-dated call granted by a company to an employee; it must vest and cannot be sold or hedged. (Defined in 5.2 Option Basics)
- **put–call parity** (put-call-parity): The no-arbitrage relation between European call and put prices, C − P = S − Ke^{−rT}. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **replicating portfolio** (replicating-portfolio): A portfolio of the underlying and borrowing whose payoff equals a derivative's in every state. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **binomial model** (binomial-model): A model that lets the price move only up or down each period and prices an option by replicating it step by step. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **risk-neutral pricing** (risk-neutral-pricing): Pricing by taking expectations with the probabilities that make the underlying earn the risk-free rate, then discounting at that rate. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **Black–Scholes model** (black-scholes-model): The pricing formula for European options when the stock price is lognormal with constant volatility. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **delta** (option-delta): The sensitivity of an option's price to the underlying price; also the amount of the underlying needed to replicate or hedge it. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **vega** (vega): The sensitivity of an option's price to volatility. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **implied volatility** (implied-volatility): The volatility that makes an option pricing model match the market price. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **volatility skew** (volatility-skew): The pattern of implied volatility across strikes for one expiry; for index options it rises as the strike falls. (Defined in 5.3 Option Pricing)
- **interest rate swap** (interest-rate-swap): A contract in which two parties exchange fixed and floating interest on a notional principal, paying only the difference. (Defined in 5.4 Swaps (Optional))
- **notional principal** (notional-principal): The amount on which swap interest is computed; not exchanged in an interest rate swap. (Defined in 5.4 Swaps (Optional))
- **swap rate** (swap-rate): The fixed rate that makes a swap worth 0 at the start; equal to the coupon rate of a par bond. (Defined in 5.4 Swaps (Optional))
- **counterparty risk** (counterparty-risk): The risk that the other party to a contract defaults and cannot make its payments. (Defined in 5.4 Swaps (Optional))
- **currency swap** (currency-swap): A contract exchanging principal and interest in two currencies, with principal exchanged at the start and at maturity. (Defined in 5.4 Swaps (Optional))
- **credit default swap** (credit-default-swap): A contract in which the protection buyer pays a yearly spread and the seller pays the loss if the reference entity defaults. (Defined in 5.4 Swaps (Optional))
- **real estate investment trust** (reit): A company that owns and runs real estate and pays out most of its income as dividends (REIT). (Defined in 5.5 Alternative Assets)
- **hedge fund** (hedge-fund): A fund for wealthy investors and institutions that may sell short and use leverage, charging management and incentive fees. (Defined in 5.5 Alternative Assets)
- **incentive fee** (incentive-fee): A fee equal to a share of a fund's returns, usually with a high-water mark. (Defined in 5.5 Alternative Assets)
- **private equity** (private-equity): Long-lived funds investing in unlisted companies; illiquid and valued by appraisal. (Defined in 5.5 Alternative Assets)
- **illiquidity premium** (illiquidity-premium): The extra return investors require for holding an asset that cannot easily be sold. (Defined in 5.5 Alternative Assets)
- **crypto asset** (crypto-asset): A digital asset recorded on a blockchain, such as bitcoin; its price is very volatile. (Defined in 5.5 Alternative Assets)
- **mutual fund** (mutual-fund): A fund pooling investors' money, invested by a manager under a stated strategy; open-end funds are bought and redeemed at NAV. (Defined in 6.1 Fund Types and Structures)
- **net asset value** (net-asset-value): A fund's assets minus liabilities divided by shares; US mutual funds compute it once a day after the close. (Defined in 6.1 Fund Types and Structures)
- **exchange-traded fund** (exchange-traded-fund): A fund whose shares trade on an exchange at market prices (ETF), created and redeemed through authorized participants. (Defined in 6.1 Fund Types and Structures)
- **creation and redemption** (creation-redemption): The mechanism by which authorized participants exchange baskets of securities for ETF shares, keeping the price near NAV. (Defined in 6.1 Fund Types and Structures)
- **capital gains distribution** (capital-gains-distribution): A fund's payout of realized capital gains, taxable to holders that year. (Defined in 6.1 Fund Types and Structures)
- **index fund** (index-fund): A fund that holds an index's members by rule, aiming to match the index's return. (Defined in 6.1 Fund Types and Structures)
- **closed-end fund** (closed-end-fund): A fund with a fixed number of shares that trade on an exchange, with no creation or redemption. (Defined in 6.1 Fund Types and Structures)
- **expense ratio** (expense-ratio): A fund's yearly operating expenses as a share of average assets, deducted daily from assets. (Defined in 6.2 Fund Costs)
- **12b-1 fee** (twelve-b-1-fee): A yearly marketing and service fee taken from fund assets, included in the expense ratio, at most 1%. (Defined in 6.2 Fund Costs)
- **turnover ratio** (turnover-ratio): The smaller of a year's purchases or sales as a share of average assets. (Defined in 6.2 Fund Costs)
- **tracking difference** (tracking-difference): The average of an index fund's return minus the index return; how much it lags on average. (Defined in 6.2 Fund Costs)
- **passive investing** (passive-investing): Holding the whole market weighted by market capitalization, without trying to pick stocks or time the market. (Defined in 6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing)
- **active management** (active-management): Trying to earn more than the market by picking stocks or timing the market. (Defined in 6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing)
- **active share** (active-share): Half the sum of absolute differences between fund and benchmark weights; how different the holdings are from the benchmark. (Defined in 6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing)
- **due diligence** (due-diligence): A systematic check of a fund's strategy, people, performance, costs and risks, before and while investing. (Defined in 6.4 A Framework for Fund Due Diligence)
- **performance attribution** (performance-attribution): Splitting excess return over a benchmark into sources such as allocation and selection effects. (Defined in 6.4 A Framework for Fund Due Diligence)
- **liquidity mismatch** (liquidity-mismatch): A fund allowing frequent redemptions while holding assets that cannot be sold quickly at reasonable prices. (Defined in 6.4 A Framework for Fund Due Diligence)
- **long-term capital gain** (long-term-capital-gain): A gain on an asset held more than one year, taxed at the lower 0%/15%/20% rates. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **qualified dividend** (qualified-dividend): A dividend from a US company meeting holding-period rules, taxed at long-term capital gains rates. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **traditional account** (traditional-account): A retirement account with tax-free contributions and growth, taxed at ordinary rates on withdrawal. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **Roth account** (roth-account): A retirement account funded with taxed money, with tax-free growth and qualified withdrawals. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **health savings account** (health-savings-account): An account paired with a high-deductible health plan (HSA); contributions, growth and medical withdrawals are tax-free. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **529 plan** (plan-529): A state education savings account with tax-free growth and qualified education withdrawals. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **backdoor Roth** (backdoor-roth): Putting nondeductible money into a traditional IRA and converting it to a Roth IRA, getting around income limits. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **restricted stock unit** (restricted-stock-unit): A grant of shares delivered at vesting (RSU), whose value then is taxed as wages. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **employee stock purchase plan** (employee-stock-purchase-plan): A plan letting employees buy company stock at a discount through payroll deductions (ESPP). (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **alternative minimum tax** (alternative-minimum-tax): A parallel income tax calculation with fewer deductions (AMT), due when higher; includes the ISO exercise spread. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **asset location** (asset-location): Deciding which accounts, by tax treatment, hold which assets. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **tax-loss harvesting** (tax-loss-harvesting): Selling losing securities to realize capital losses for tax, while buying similar assets to keep exposure. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **wash sale rule** (wash-sale-rule): A loss cannot be deducted that year if substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after the sale. (Defined in 6.5 Accounts and Taxes (US))
- **household balance sheet** (household-balance-sheet): A list of a household's financial assets, real assets, human capital and liabilities. (Defined in 6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance)
- **emergency fund** (emergency-fund): Money kept stable and available for job loss, illness and unexpected costs. (Defined in 6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance)
- **term life insurance** (term-life-insurance): Life insurance paying the face amount if the insured dies within the agreed term. (Defined in 6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance)
- **disability insurance** (disability-insurance): Insurance paying part of income monthly when illness or injury prevents work. (Defined in 6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance)
- **beneficiary designation** (beneficiary-designation): Naming who receives a retirement account or insurance on the owner's death, outside the will. (Defined in 6.6 The Household Balance Sheet and Insurance)
- **strategic asset allocation** (strategic-asset-allocation): The long-term target mix set by goals, risk capacity and tolerance, and capital market assumptions. (Defined in 6.7 Asset Allocation)
- **tactical asset allocation** (tactical-asset-allocation): A temporary departure from the strategic mix on a short-term market view; in effect market timing. (Defined in 6.7 Asset Allocation)
- **home bias** (home-bias): Investors holding far more domestic assets than the home market's share of the global market. (Defined in 6.7 Asset Allocation)
- **rebalancing** (rebalancing): Selling overweight and buying underweight assets to bring the portfolio back to target. (Defined in 6.7 Asset Allocation)
- **Form 10-K** (form-10-k): The audited annual report US listed companies file with the SEC. (Defined in 6.8 The Stock Research Process)
- **five forces** (five-forces): Porter's framework for industry profits: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, supplier power and buyer power. (Defined in 6.8 The Stock Research Process)
- **reverse DCF** (reverse-dcf): Working back from today's price to the future growth the market implies. (Defined in 6.8 The Stock Research Process)
- **investment thesis** (investment-thesis): A written case for why price is below value, how one differs from the market, and what would prove one wrong. (Defined in 6.8 The Stock Research Process)
- **replacement ratio** (replacement-ratio): Retirement spending (or income) as a share of pre-retirement income. (Defined in 6.9 Retirement Planning)
- **safe withdrawal rate** (safe-withdrawal-rate): The first-year withdrawal share, raised with inflation after, that very likely lasts the planned horizon. (Defined in 6.9 Retirement Planning)
- **sequence-of-returns risk** (sequence-of-returns-risk): The risk that, during withdrawals, the same returns in a different order give very different outcomes. (Defined in 6.9 Retirement Planning)
- **full retirement age** (full-retirement-age): The age at which full Social Security benefits are paid; 67 for those born 1960 or later. (Defined in 6.9 Retirement Planning)
- **longevity risk** (longevity-risk): The risk of living longer than planned and running out of money. (Defined in 6.9 Retirement Planning)
- **time-weighted return** (time-weighted-return): The geometric average of period returns for a lump sum held throughout; what funds report. (Defined in 6.10 Risk Management and Common Mistakes)
- **dollar-weighted return** (dollar-weighted-return): The return that accounts for the timing and size of each purchase and withdrawal; the IRR of the cash flows. (Defined in 6.10 Risk Management and Common Mistakes)
- **investment policy statement** (investment-policy-statement): A document stating a household's goals, horizon, risk capacity, allocation and rules (IPS). (Defined in 6.10 Risk Management and Common Mistakes)
- **money illusion** (money-illusion): The tendency to think in nominal amounts rather than real purchasing power. (Defined in 6.11 Inflation and Real Returns)
- **I bond** (i-bond): A US Treasury savings bond whose rate combines a fixed rate and a CPI-based inflation rate; its nominal value never falls. (Defined in 6.11 Inflation and Real Returns)
- **goals-based investing** (goals-based-investing): Treating each household goal as a liability with an amount, date and importance, and matching assets to each. (Defined in 6.12 Goals-Based Investing)
- **funded ratio** (funded-ratio): Assets set aside for a goal divided by the goal's present value at the riskless rate. (Defined in 6.12 Goals-Based Investing)
- **annual review** (annual-review): A yearly check, against a fixed list, of the household's balance sheet, goals, allocation, costs, taxes, protection and IPS. (Defined in 6.13 Monitoring and Review)
- **decision journal** (decision-journal): A written record, at each important decision, of information, reasoning, expectations and exit conditions, for judging reasoning rather than outcomes. (Defined in 6.13 Monitoring and Review)
